docs.title: systemspec-crypto
docs.text:
A Go-first, machine-readable intermediate representation for describing the cryptography a system uses: what crypto exists, where and why it is used, how it is configured and managed, and what evidence supports those claims.

The IR is the source of truth, not an LLM. The spec holds facts and evidence, never prose answers. Questionnaire responses, posture findings, and CycloneDX CBOM documents are projections over it; anything the IR cannot support is "not currently documented," never invented.

docs.title: Why systemspec-crypto?
docs.text:
Security questionnaires, audits, and architecture reviews ask endless variations of the same cryptography questions, and the answers go stale the moment the code changes. An SBOM/CBOM tells you that an algorithm exists somewhere; it does not tell you why, where, or how it is used, or what evidence backs the claim. This model fills that gap:

  • Capabilities are not usage — an implementation records what it can do separately from what the system actually does with it, so no consumer can infer use of a capability merely because a library supports it.
  • Facts carry verification — every claim records a state (discovered → inferred → review-required → verified → attested), so an AI-inferred fact and a human-attested one stay distinguishable.
  • Uses are the heart — one Use ties an algorithm to a purpose, component, configuration, locations, and evidence, answering many differently-worded questions from a single record.
  • Findings are not facts — cryptographic posture is evaluated by a separate, policy-driven linter whose findings are ephemeral; a library can gain a CVE tomorrow without the spec changing.

The primary responsibility of this project is the semantic model itself. Answer generation, posture linting, and CBOM exchange are consumers of the spec, not the spec. See the Specification for the full normative model.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
go install github.com/plexusone/systemspec-crypto/cmd/cryptospec@latest

cryptospec validate crypto.json                 # structural validation
cryptospec report   crypto.json                 # human-readable summary
cryptospec cbom export crypto.json -o crypto.cbom.json

The same commands mount under a family aggregate CLI as systemspec crypto ….

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Initial release of systemspec-crypto: a Go-first, machine-readable IR describing the cryptography a system uses as facts and evidence, never prose. Implementations separate capabilities (what they can do) from usedCapabilities (what the system does with them), and every claim carries a verification state (discovered → inferred → review-required → verified → attested).
  • A cryptospec CLI validates a spec against structural rules and reports a human-readable summary; the same subcommands mount under a family aggregate CLI via NewRootCommand/NewCommand.
  • Dogfooded end to end on the public plexusone/omniagent platform (Argon2id passwords, SHA-256 token hashing, ECDSA/RSA JWT verification, crypto/rand CSPRNG), and exported to a CycloneDX 1.6 CBOM.

docs.title: systemspec-crypto Specification v0.1
docs.text:
This document is the normative specification of the systemspec-crypto data model, describing what is true of the cryptospec package's types and the JSON documents they marshal to and from.

systemspec-crypto describes the cryptography a system uses as facts and evidence, never prose answers. A Spec records the cryptographic implementations a system relies on, the algorithms they provide, the uses that tie an algorithm to a purpose and place, and the claims — each backed by evidence and carrying a verification state — asserted about them. Questionnaire answers, posture findings, and CycloneDX CBOM documents are computed from this model; none of them are the model. The primary responsibility of this specification is the semantic model itself.

Two invariants govern the model:

  • Capabilities are not usage. An implementation separates what it can do from what the system does with it, so no consumer may infer use of a cryptographic capability merely because an implementation supports it.
  • Facts carry verification. Every claim records how strongly it is known, so an AI-inferred fact and a human-attested fact remain distinguishable.

Every type in this specification conforms to the PlexusOne static-type profile: no oneOf, anyOf, allOf, or other JSON Schema composition, and no untyped or heterogeneous maps. Controlled vocabularies are expressed as string enums and optional data as explicit named fields, so the canonical Go model and its generated JSON Schema remain structurally isomorphic. The generated schema is schema/crypto.schema.json; it passes schemakit lint --property-case camelCase with zero findings.

docs.title: 1. Spec Document
docs.text:
A Spec is the top-level systemspec-crypto document.

specVersion      the spec FORMAT version, e.g. "0.1.0" (§1.1). Required.
metadata         descriptive facts about the document (name, description, timestamps)
system           the system this spec describes (§1.2). Required.
scope            what release/environment/components the spec covers (§1.3)
implementations  the cryptographic implementations the system relies on (§3)
algorithms       the algorithm registry (§4)
uses             how algorithms are used (§5)
claims           asserted, verifiable statements about the above (§6)
evidence         locators supporting claims (§7)

docs.title: 1.1 Spec version
docs.text: specVersion is the semantic version of the spec format, not of the described system. Documents conforming to this specification carry "0.1.0". Additive format changes increment the minor version; breaking changes increment the major version. Tooling MUST accept any document whose major version it understands.

docs.title: 1.2 System identity
docs.text:
id    an opaque, stable identifier for the described system. Required.
name  human-readable system name

SystemRef is deliberately minimal in v0.1. A structured, family-wide identifier scheme is a later decision; id remains a string so adopting one never breaks a v0.1 document.

docs.title: 1.3 Scope
docs.text:
release      the released version described, e.g. "1.8.2"
environment  e.g. "production"
components   opaque component identifiers owned by the described system

Scope lets one system be described at a specific release while another revision carries different cryptography.

docs.title: 2. Identity and References
docs.text:
Object id values are lowercase kebab-case slugs carrying a type prefix and MUST be unique within a Spec:

impl:<slug>        an implementation
algorithm:<slug>   an algorithm
use:<slug>         a use
claim:<slug>       a claim
evidence:<slug>    an evidence entry

Reference fields (algorithmRef, implementationRef, evidenceRefs, targetRefs) hold these IDs verbatim and MUST resolve to an object of the expected type (§9). roadmapRefs are the exception: they are opaque external roadmap-item identifiers and are never resolved by this specification. Detailed planning MUST NOT be embedded in the Spec; a Spec references planned work by ID only.

docs.title: 3. Implementations
docs.text:
An Implementation is a mechanism that provides cryptography. A library is only one kind.

id                stable identity (§2). Required.
type              classification from the closed vocabulary (§3.1). Required.
name              human-readable name. Required.
version           implementation version, e.g. "go1.26", "v0.56.0"
provider          the providing vendor or platform, where applicable
capabilities      what this implementation CAN do (§3.2)
usedCapabilities  what this system DOES with it (§3.2)
lifecycle         temporal state (§8)
evidenceRefs      supporting evidence IDs (§7)

docs.title: 3.1 Type taxonomy
docs.text:
library     runtime     operating-system   cloud-provider   kms
hsm         tpm         database           service          hardware
external

docs.title: 3.2 Capabilities versus used capabilities
docs.text:
capabilities and usedCapabilities are free-text capability labels (e.g. "SHA-256", "AES-256-GCM"). capabilities records what the implementation is able to do; usedCapabilities records what this system actually uses. This separation is the model's central anti-hallucination control: a scanner or language model MUST NOT convert "the implementation supports X" into "the system uses X".

When capabilities is non-empty, every entry of usedCapabilities MUST also appear in capabilities (§9). When capabilities is empty the containment check does not apply — an implementation whose full capability set is not enumerated (for example a managed KMS or HSM) may still declare what it is used for.

docs.title: 4. Algorithms
docs.text:
An Algorithm is a normalized registry entry describing what a cryptographic primitive is. It never describes how the system uses the primitive; that is a Use (§5).

id         stable identity (§2). Required.
name       common name, e.g. "SHA-256", "AES-256-GCM". Required.
class      classification from the closed vocabulary (§4.1). Required.
standard   the defining standard, e.g. "FIPS 180-4", "RFC 9106"
keySize    key size in bits, where applicable
lifecycle  temporal state (§8)

docs.title: 4.1 Class taxonomy
docs.text:
hash                      mac                    symmetric-encryption
authenticated-encryption  asymmetric-encryption  signature
kdf                       password-hash          key-agreement
kem                       randomness

docs.title: 5. Uses
docs.text:
A Use is the heart of the Spec. A cryptographic inventory can record that an algorithm exists; a Use records that the algorithm is used for a given purpose, in a given component, with a given configuration, at given locations, backed by given evidence. One Use answers many differently-worded questions.

id                 stable identity (§2). Required.
purpose            why the algorithm is used, from the closed vocabulary (§5.1). Required.
description        prose description of the use
algorithmRef       the algorithm used; MUST resolve to an Algorithm (§4). Required.
implementationRef  the implementation providing it; MUST resolve to an Implementation (§3)
component          the component identifier where the use occurs
data               classification of the protected data (§5.2)
configuration      configuration parameters (§5.3)
locations          where the use is realized (§5.4)
standards          applicable standards, e.g. ["RFC 9106"]
lifecycle          temporal state (§8)
roadmapRefs        opaque roadmap-item IDs (§2)
evidenceRefs       supporting evidence IDs (§7)

docs.title: 5.1 Purpose vocabulary
docs.text:
purpose is a closed vocabulary. other with a description is the escape hatch, so authors never invent near-synonyms.

integrity        confidentiality   authentication   signing
key-derivation   credential-protection   randomness   other

docs.title: 5.2 Data context
docs.text:
classification  the class of protected data, e.g. "credentials", "customer-data". Required.
description     prose description

docs.title: 5.3 Configuration
docs.text:
salted      tri-state: unset = not documented, false = explicitly unsalted, true = salted
iterations  work factor / iteration count, where applicable
parameters  a homogeneous string map of additional named parameters

parameters carries configuration a questionnaire asks about that has no explicit field — for example an Argon2 memory/parallelism parameter set. It is a map[string]string: a fixed value type, permitted under the static-type profile, never a heterogeneous or untyped map.

docs.title: 5.4 Locations
docs.text:
A Location is a locator for where a use is realized, never the evidence content itself.

type        one of: source | config | deployment | runtime. Required.
repository  the repository, where applicable
path        file or resource path
symbol      the symbol (function, type) within the path

docs.title: 6. Claims and Verification
docs.text:
A Claim is a stated assertion about the system's cryptography, backed by evidence and carrying a verification state. Claims are the verification surface of the Spec. Inventory objects (implementations, algorithms, uses) carry evidenceRefs only; they do not carry their own verification status. Consumers and future implementations MUST NOT add per-object verification: a single claim, which may cover several objects via targetRefs, is the one place a verification state lives, so a fact and its covering claim can never disagree.

id            stable identity (§2). Required.
type          claim category, e.g. "crypto-usage"
statement     the human-readable assertion. Required.
targetRefs    IDs of the uses/implementations/algorithms this claim covers;
              each MUST resolve to one of those object types (§9)
verification  the verification state (§6.1). Required.
evidenceRefs  supporting evidence IDs (§7)

docs.title: 6.1 Verification state machine
docs.text:
status      one of the states below. Required.
method      how the state was reached, e.g. "source-analysis"
verifiedBy  the person or team, where applicable
verifiedAt  an RFC 3339 timestamp, where applicable

status is one of, in increasing strength:

discovered → inferred → review-required → verified → attested

A consumer generating an external statement SHOULD gate on the state: a verified or attested claim may be stated as current fact; inferred or review-required claims must be qualified or held for review; discovered claims are supporting evidence only. A claim whose status is verified or attested MUST carry at least one evidenceRef (§9). v0.1 records any state; auditing of transitions between states is the responsibility of tooling that writes the Spec.

docs.title: 7. Evidence and Provenance
docs.text:
An Evidence entry is a locator for something that supports a claim. The Spec stores pointers to evidence, never the evidence content.

id          stable identity (§2). Required.
type        classification from the closed vocabulary (§7.1). Required.
repository  the repository, where applicable
path        file or resource path
symbol      the symbol within the path
uri         a URI locator, where applicable
provenance  how the evidence entered the Spec (§7.2)

docs.title: 7.1 Evidence type taxonomy
docs.text:
source-code       dependency        configuration      iac
runtime-observation   tls-scan      sbom               cbom
cloud-configuration   certificate   test               documentation
human-attestation     vendor-documentation

docs.title: 7.2 Provenance
docs.text:
method      how the assertion entered the Spec (§7.2.1)
analyzer    the tool or person identifier
analyzedAt  an RFC 3339 timestamp

docs.title: 7.2.1 Provenance method
docs.text:
static-analyzer   llm-analyzer   sbom-import
scanner           developer      security-review

Provenance keeps "a static analyzer found this", "a language model inferred this", "a scanner observed this", and "a reviewer recorded this" distinguishable, which matters for any customer-facing projection of the facts.

docs.title: 8. Lifecycle
docs.text:
Lifecycle is a shared temporal-state primitive that lets any object say "I am not current" without embedding a roadmap.

status      one of: proposed | planned | in-progress | available |
                    deprecated | retired | cancelled
introduced  the release/version an object became current
deprecated  the release/version an object was deprecated
removed     the release/version an object was removed

Detailed delivery planning (dates, milestones, dependencies) lives in roadmap items referenced by roadmapRefs, never inline.

docs.title: 9. Validation
docs.text:
The validate package checks a Spec against these always-on structural rules. An error-severity finding means the Spec is invalid; a warning is advisory. A valid Spec produces no findings.

required fields     specVersion, system.id, and each object's required fields present
id conventions      every id carries the prefix matching its object type (§2)
id uniqueness       object ids are unique within the Spec
reference resolves  algorithmRef, implementationRef, evidenceRefs, and targetRefs
                    resolve to objects of the expected type
capability containment
                    when an implementation enumerates capabilities, its
                    usedCapabilities are a subset of them (§3.2)
usage justification (warning)
                    an implementation declaring usedCapabilities is referenced by
                    at least one Use
vocabulary          lifecycle status, provenance method, implementation type,
                    algorithm class, use purpose, location type, evidence type,
                    and verification status are within their controlled vocabularies
evidence required   a claim whose verification status is verified or attested
                    carries at least one evidenceRef (§6.1)

Cryptographic posture — whether an algorithm is weak, a library outdated, or a configuration noncompliant — is out of scope for validation. Posture is the responsibility of a later, policy-driven linter whose findings are ephemeral and kept separate from the Spec.

docs.title: 10. CycloneDX CBOM Export
docs.text:
The cbom package projects a Spec into a CycloneDX 1.6 CBOM: the system as an application component, each implementation as a library, and each algorithm as a cryptographic-asset whose primitive is mapped from its class. The Spec's uses drive a dependency graph in which implementations provide algorithms.

CBOM models cryptographic inventory but not usage purpose, configuration, locations, claims, evidence, or verification state. Export is therefore a lossy projection, and it MUST report the facts it drops rather than losing them silently. CBOM is an interchange peer, never a replacement for this model.

docs.title: 11. Non-goals (v0.1)
docs.text:
• Answer generation. Mapping questionnaire wording onto Spec facts and writing prose is a downstream consumer, out of scope for this repository.
  • Key, certificate, protocol, and data-protection detail. Key classes, PKI, protocol cryptography, and at-rest/in-transit protection records are reserved for a later revision.
  • CBOM import and round-trip fixtures. v0.1 exports only.
  • Posture linting and policy profiles (FIPS, PCI, and similar). Reserved for a later, policy-driven linter with ephemeral findings.
  • Crypto agility, PQC assessment, RAS characteristics, and disclosure-policy projections. Reserved.
  • Secrets storage. The model describes key classes and management practices only; no field may ever hold key material, secret values, or operational credentials. This is a permanent invariant, not a deferred feature.
  • Threat and risk analysis. Threats, mitigations, and findings belong to tooling that consumes this Spec.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text: The facts-and-evidence model with a verification state machine draws on the same claim/evidence philosophy used across the PlexusOne spec family. Cryptographic inventory interchange is delegated to CycloneDX CBOM (github.com/CycloneDX/cyclonedx-go) rather than reinvented; this specification's differentiation is the usage, configuration, evidence, and verification layer that CBOM does not model. The Go-first schema workflow (invopop/jsonschema generation linted by grokify/schemakit) and the composable Cobra CLI follow the conventions established by the sibling systems-spec family specifications.

docs.title: Release Notes: v0.1.0
docs.text: Release Date: 2026-09-08

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
Initial release of systemspec-crypto: a Go-first, machine-readable intermediate representation for describing the cryptography a system uses — what crypto exists, where and why it is used, how it is configured, and what evidence supports those claims. The IR holds facts and evidence, never prose answers; questionnaire responses, posture findings, and CycloneDX CBOM documents are projections over it.

Two invariants shape the model and make it safe to build on:

  • Capabilities are not usage. An implementation records what it can do (capabilities) separately from what the system actually does with it (usedCapabilities), so a scanner or language model can never turn "the library supports X" into "the product uses X".
  • Facts carry verification. Every claim records a verification state (discovered → inferred → review-required → verified → attested), so an AI-inferred fact and a human-attested one stay distinguishable.

Dogfooded end to end on the public plexusone/omniagent platform and exported to a CycloneDX 1.6 CBOM.

docs.title: Core IR
docs.text:
cryptospec.Spec is the canonical document: Implementation, Algorithm, Use, Claim, Evidence, plus the shared Lifecycle, Provenance, and Verification primitives. See the Specification for the full normative model.

import "github.com/plexusone/systemspec-crypto/cryptospec"

spec := cryptospec.Spec{
    SpecVersion: cryptospec.SpecVersion,
    System:      cryptospec.SystemRef{ID: "example-service", Name: "Example Service"},
    Implementations: []cryptospec.Implementation{{
        ID:               "impl:go-stdlib",
        Type:             cryptospec.ImplementationLibrary,
        Name:             "Go standard crypto",
        Capabilities:     []string{"SHA-256", "AES-256-GCM"},
        UsedCapabilities: []string{"SHA-256"},
    }},
    Algorithms: []cryptospec.Algorithm{{
        ID: "algorithm:sha-256", Name: "SHA-256", Class: cryptospec.ClassHash,
    }},
    Uses: []cryptospec.Use{{
        ID: "use:artifact-integrity", Purpose: cryptospec.PurposeIntegrity,
        AlgorithmRef: "algorithm:sha-256", ImplementationRef: "impl:go-stdlib",
    }},
}

docs.title: The Use object
docs.text: A cryptographic inventory can say SHA-256 exists; a Use says SHA-256 is used for artifact integrity, in a given component, with a given configuration (salt/iterations/parameters), at given source locations, backed by given evidence. One Use answers many differently-worded questions.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: validate.Validate checks referential integrity, usedCapabilities ⊆ capabilities (when capabilities are enumerated), controlled-vocabulary conformance, type-prefixed ID conventions and uniqueness, and the requirement that verified/attested claims carry evidence. Cryptographic posture (weak algorithms, outdated libraries) is deliberately out of scope — that is a later, policy-driven linter whose findings are ephemeral and kept out of the spec.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
go install github.com/plexusone/systemspec-crypto/cmd/cryptospec@v0.1.0

cryptospec validate crypto.json                 # structural rules; non-zero exit on errors
cryptospec report   crypto.json                 # human-readable internal summary
cryptospec cbom export crypto.json -o crypto.cbom.json   # CycloneDX 1.6 CBOM

The same commands mount under a family aggregate CLI as systemspec crypto … via cli.NewCommand(); all capability lives in importable packages, with cmd/cryptospec a thin adapter.

docs.title: Go-first schema
docs.text: Go structs are the source of truth. schema/crypto.schema.json is generated from them and passes schemakit lint --property-case camelCase with zero findings, guaranteeing the model maps cleanly to statically-typed languages.

docs.title: CycloneDX CBOM export
docs.text: cryptospec cbom export projects a spec into a CycloneDX 1.6 CBOM — the system as an application, implementations as libraries, algorithms as cryptographic-asset components. Because CBOM cannot carry usage purpose, configuration, evidence, or verification state, the export is a lossy projection and reports what it drops rather than losing it silently.

docs.title: Dogfood
docs.text: examples/dogfood/omniagent.json describes the cryptography of the public plexusone/omniagent platform, discovered by source analysis: Argon2id password hashing, SHA-256 token hashing, ECDSA/RSA JWT signature verification, crypto/rand CSPRNG, and gorilla cookie authentication. Every fact carries an evidence locator and a verification state; the library-default session cookie MAC is honestly recorded as inferred rather than verified.

docs.title: Conformance
docs.text:
• A shared fixture corpus under examples/fixtures/{valid,invalid} is exercised by both the Go validator and JSON Schema validation; valid fixtures also round-trip Go → JSON → schema without loss.
  • go test ./..., golangci-lint, and schemakit lint all run clean in CI.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text: Key management, certificates, protocols, and data-protection detail; CBOM import; the posture linter; and crypto-agility / PQC / RAS / disclosure models are planned for later revisions — see the ROADMAP. The spec never stores secret material; that is a permanent invariant.

docs.title: PLAN — systemspec-crypto — Machine-Readable Cryptography Evidence IR (v0.1)
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-SYSTEMSPECCRYPTO-001

docs.title: Sequencing Rationale
docs.text:
The sequencing optimizes for the first real user — our own Go application portfolio — and its nearest payoff: a complete, evidence-backed cryptographic description of a real application that can answer questionnaire-style questions purely from the IR. Everything else (CBOM exchange, posture linting, disclosure views) is a consumer of that description and ships after it exists and has been proven on a real system.

Phase 1 locks the core inventory model (shared primitives, implementations, algorithms, uses) because the IR is the hardest part to retrofit — and because capabilities vs usedCapabilities and the Use object are the design decisions everything downstream depends on. Phase 2 adds the claims/evidence/verification layer and the schema pipeline, then validation, because facts without verification states are exactly the hallucination surface this spec exists to eliminate. Phase 3 delivers the CLI, the dogfood spec, and the v0.1 release.

Post-v0.1: Phase 4 extends the descriptive model to keys, certificates, protocols, and data protections — deliberately deferred because those objects are additive and benefit from authoring experience with the core. Phase 5 adds the review, expectation and operating-mode fields that producers of declared facts need, so a declaration cannot outlive its review. Phase 6 builds the CycloneDX CBOM bridge (interchange, never reinvention). Phase 7 builds the posture linter with configurable policy and ephemeral findings. Phase 8 (crypto agility, PQC assessment, RAS, disclosure views) is demand-paced: each model grows from real questionnaire and review needs rather than an empty taxonomy built upfront. Phase 9 adds semantic diff and change impact.

docs.title: Phases
docs.text:
1. Core Inventory Model — shared primitives (Lifecycle, Provenance, ID/ref conventions), spec envelope with system identity and scope, implementations with capabilities vs usedCapabilities, algorithm registry, uses. Exit: a hand-authored spec for a small real system parses with all core object types populated.
  2. Evidence, Verification & Schema Pipeline — evidence model, claims with the verification state machine, generated schemas linted by schemakit, embedded, validation rules, fixture corpus with round-trip tests. Exit: schemas lint clean; the validator rejects a usedCapabilities ⊄ capabilities fixture and an unresolved-reference fixture with actionable messages.
  3. CLI & Dogfood (closes v0.1) — cli package with root/subcommand constructors, cryptospec validate and cryptospec report, dogfood spec for a real Go application, v0.1 release with SPEC.md, README, CI, tag. Exit: canonical questionnaire questions answered purely by querying the dogfood IR, every answer traceable to evidence; v0.1 tagged.
  4. Key Management & Protocol Model (v0.2 candidate) — key classes (never secret values), certificates/PKI, protocol cryptography, data protections, key-management providers with standards conformance (NIST SP 800-57, KMIP, PKCS#11, X9 family). Exit: the dogfood spec describes its TLS posture, key classes, and supported key-management standards end to end.
  5. Review, Expectation & Operating Mode — review fields on verification (reviewBy, reviewedAt, reviewedBy) with expiry derived at read time, owned expectations at or above the policy floor with a waiver form, operating mode and module validation on implementations, a per-use algorithm profile, and a dated key-state summary convention. Exit: a declared external boundary is expressed as an owned expectation with a review date, goes review-required when the date passes, and a below-floor expectation is representable only as a waiver.
  6. CBOM Bridge — artifact references, CycloneDX CBOM import and export, mapping fixtures. Exit: round-trip against real CycloneDX CBOM examples with lossy conversions reported, never silent.
  7. Posture Linter & Policy — policy model, ephemeral findings separate from spec facts, rule engine distinguishing capability risk from configured risk (including conditional-pass / secure-configuration-required), lint profiles, cryptospec lint. Exit: the dogfood spec lints against two different profiles producing different findings from the same facts.
  8. Agility, PQC, RAS & Disclosure (demand-paced) — crypto-agility model, PQC assessments over existing uses with roadmap references, crypto-specific RAS characteristics, disclosure-policy views for report. Exit: internal and external reports generated from the same spec with field-level disclosure control.
  9. Semantic Diff & Change Impact — typed change sets over a spec, framework-neutral impact classification, and a diff command. Exit: two versions of the dogfood spec produce a change set and impacts with CI-gate exit codes.

docs.title: Milestones
docs.text:
• M1 (end Phase 2): a real spec file round-trips through the full pipeline; schemas lint clean; validator catches the canonical invalid fixtures.
  • M2 (end Phase 3, v0.1): the dogfood application's cryptography is fully described and queryable; questionnaire-style questions answered from the IR alone; v0.1 tagged.
  • M3 (end Phase 6): CBOM import/export round-trips against CycloneDX examples.
  • M4 (end Phase 7): cryptospec lint produces a defensible posture report for the dogfood spec under multiple profiles.

docs.title: Risks & Mitigations
docs.text:
• Model bloat / trying to be four specs at once. The spec answers one question (what crypto exists, why/where/how, how managed, what evidence). Threat analysis, operational RAS beyond crypto-specific characteristics, and planning data are explicitly out of scope; every proposed field must serve description or evidence, not analysis output.
  • Use authoring burden kills adoption. We are the first user; the dogfood spec is the authoring-UX test. If modeling a real application feels painful, the schema changes, not the example.
  • Verification states get ignored and everything becomes "verified." validate requires evidence on verified/attested claims; provenance records who/what asserted each fact, keeping AI-inferred and human-attested distinguishable.
  • Spec drifts into a findings store. Lint findings are ephemeral artifacts produced by a later-phase consumer; the invariant "a library can gain a CVE tomorrow without the spec changing" is enforced by keeping vulnerability/posture output out of the schema.
  • Premature shared-module extraction across the family. Shared primitives stay local until a second family member needs them; extraction is a recorded later decision, avoiding lockstep versioning.
  • CBOM bridge scope creep. The bridge maps, it does not model; anything CycloneDX already represents well is imported/exported, not duplicated in the core.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Commits carry Refs: RMI-SYSTEMSPECCRYPTO-NNN trailers; phases are reviewed and executed as units; phase status derives from member RMIs.
  • Go-first schema workflow per org conventions: invopop/jsonschema generation, schemakit lint --property-case camelCase, //go:embed, tools.go guard for generator deps.
  • Pre-push: go test ./..., golangci-lint run, coverage badge per global checklist.

docs.title: PRD — systemspec-crypto — Machine-Readable Cryptography Evidence IR (v0.1)
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-SYSTEMSPECCRYPTO-001 Home repo: github.com/plexusone/systemspec-crypto Status: proposed

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Security questionnaires, DDQs, architecture reviews, procurement requests, and audits ask endless slight variations of the same cryptography questions: which hash algorithms and why, what encrypts data at rest and in transit, which libraries are used and how are they configured, how are keys managed, what is the PQC plan. Today the answers live in spreadsheets and prose documents that go stale the moment the code changes. SBOM/CBOM inventories tell you that SHA-256 or AES-256-GCM exists somewhere in the dependency tree, but not why, where, or how it is used, how the keys behind it are managed, or what evidence supports any of it. And asking an LLM to answer directly from a codebase invites the most dangerous failure mode in this space: "the library supports algorithm X, therefore the product uses X."

docs.title: Vision
docs.text:
The IR is the source of truth, not the LLM. systemspec-crypto is a vendor-neutral, Go-first JSON intermediate representation that answers one question about a system:

What cryptography does this system use, where and why does it use it, how is it configured and managed, what is its lifecycle state, and what evidence supports those claims?

The spec holds facts and evidence, never prose answers. Downstream consumers — questionnaire answer generation, posture linting, CBOM exchange, architecture review — are projections over those facts and are explicitly out of scope for this repository. A generated answer must be supportable by claims and evidence in the IR; anything the IR cannot support is "not currently documented," never invented.

Responsibility hierarchy: the primary responsibility of this project is the semantic model itself. Consumers (answer generators, linters, CBOM tooling) determine what the model must be able to express and prove it works, but they are consumers of the spec, not the spec. When a use case needs something the model can't express, the model changes; when a use case wants something only it needs, that lives in the consumer — never in the core.

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
• Product builders / security engineers (primary): maintain one authoritative, machine-readable description of a system's cryptography instead of re-answering the same questionnaire every quarter. The first user is us: the maintainers' own Go application portfolio is the dogfood corpus.
  • Security architects and reviewers: review cryptographic posture as structured facts with evidence, not tribal knowledge; review changes to the cryptographic description instead of re-auditing from scratch.
  • Compliance owners: trace every external statement back to a claim, its evidence, and its verification state.
  • AI analyzers and agents: propose spec updates from source, dependency, and configuration analysis — as discovered/inferred facts that humans verify. AI discovers; humans attest.
  • Downstream tooling: CycloneDX CBOM ecosystems (via a later import/export bridge), posture linters, and answer-generation systems consume the IR.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. Facts-and-evidence core: implementations, algorithms, and uses as typed domain objects, with claims, evidence, and provenance attached to every significant assertion.
  2. Anti-hallucination semantics: an implementation's capabilities (what it can do) and usedCapabilities (what this system actually does with it) are separate fields — the single most important control in the model. Verification is a first-class state machine (discovered → inferred → review-required → verified → attested), so consumers can apply policies like "state as fact only if verified or attested."
  3. Uses are the heart of the spec: a CBOM can say SHA-256 exists; a Use says SHA-256 is used for artifact integrity, in which component, with what configuration (salt, iterations, parameters), at which locations, backed by which evidence. One Use record answers many differently-worded questions.
  4. Statically typed friendly: Go structs are the source of truth; JSON Schema is generated (invopop/jsonschema, linted by schemakit, camelCase properties) and stays within the static-type profile — no oneOf/anyOf/allOf, explicit discriminated fields.
  5. Shared primitives, family-ready: lifecycle vocabulary (proposed/planned/in-progress/available/deprecated/retired/cancelled), evidence, provenance, and reference conventions are defined locally in this module now, designed for later extraction into a shared family root module.
  6. Composable CLI: library-first packages with a thin Cobra cli package exposing both a standalone root command (cryptospec) and a subcommand constructor, so a future family-level aggregate CLI can mount it with one import.

docs.title: Non-Goals (v0.1)
docs.text:
• Answer generation — mapping questionnaire wording onto IR facts and writing prose is a downstream consumer, permanently out of scope for this repo.
  • Key, certificate, protocol, and data-protection detail — key classes, PKI, TLS configuration, and at-rest/in-transit protection records are the first post-v0.1 phase, not v0.1.
  • CBOM bridge — CycloneDX CBOM is an import/export bridge in a later phase; it is never reinvented and never becomes the internal model.
  • Posture linter and policy profiles (FIPS/PCI/NIST-aligned/etc.) — later phase. Lint findings will be ephemeral artifacts evaluated against configurable policy, never stored as spec facts.
  • Crypto agility, rich PQC assessment, RAS characteristics, disclosure-policy projections — later phases, driven by real modeling demand.
  • Secrets storage — the spec describes key classes and management practices; it must never contain key material, secret values, or operational credentials. This is a permanent invariant, not a phase.
  • Threat and risk analysis — threats, mitigations, and findings belong to threat-model tooling that consumes this spec.
  • Roadmap/planning fields — planned work is referenced by roadmap item ID; the spec never embeds its own project-management format.

docs.title: Key Product Decisions
docs.text:
• capabilities ≠ usedCapabilities. Modeling what a library supports separately from what the system actually uses prevents scanners and LLMs from converting library capability into product behavior claims.
  • Verification state machine is first-class. Every claim carries a verification status; "AI inferred this," "a scanner observed this," "an engineer verified this," and "the security team attested this" are different facts and must remain distinguishable.
  • Uses over inventories. The algorithm registry says what a primitive is; the Use object says how the system employs it. Design effort concentrates on Use.
  • Findings are not facts. A library can be secure today and have a CVE tomorrow without the spec changing. Posture evaluation output lives outside the spec and expires; the spec describes the system.
  • Key classes, never secrets. Descriptive metadata only, from day one.
  • CBOM is an interchange peer, not a foundation. The differentiation of this spec is usage + configuration + management + evidence + verification; inventory interchange delegates to CycloneDX.
  • Shared lifecycle vocabulary across the family: proposed | planned | in-progress | available | deprecated | retired | cancelled, with detailed planning living in roadmap references (roadmapRefs), never inline.
  • Library-first, composable Cobra. Core packages carry all capability; cmd/cryptospec is a thin adapter; the cli package exposes NewRootCommand() and NewCommand() so a family aggregate CLI can mount crypto as a subcommand.
  • Go-first schema generation per org conventions: invopop/jsonschema, schemakit lint --property-case camelCase, //go:embed, tools.go guard.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
• A complete v0.1 spec file fully describes the cryptography of at least one real Go application: its crypto libraries with capabilities vs used capabilities, its algorithms, and every significant use with purpose, configuration, locations, and evidence.
  • Canonical questionnaire questions — "Which hash algorithms are used, for what purpose, with what configuration, and where?", "Which cryptographic libraries does the product employ and which of their capabilities are actually used?" — are answerable purely by querying the IR of the dogfood spec, with every answer traceable to evidence.
  • cryptospec validate enforces referential integrity, usedCapabilities ⊆ capabilities, and verification-state validity; invalid fixtures fail with actionable messages.
  • Generated JSON Schema passes schemakit lint --property-case camelCase with zero violations; Go ↔ JSON round-trip fixtures pass in CI.
  • The cli package mounts cleanly as both a standalone cryptospec binary and a subcommand constructor, verified by a test that builds an aggregate root command.

docs.title: TRD — systemspec-crypto — Machine-Readable Cryptography Evidence IR (v0.1)
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-SYSTEMSPECCRYPTO-001

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
Source / dependencies / config / SBOM / runtime evidence
      │  discovery & analysis (AI or scanner — out of repo scope)
      ▼
Proposed facts (discovered / inferred)
      │  human review
      ▼
cryptospec JSON IR  ◄── Go structs (source of truth)
      │                   │ invopop/jsonschema
      │                   ▼
      │              JSON Schema — schemakit lint --property-case camelCase — //go:embed
      │
      ├──► validate: referential integrity + semantic rules
      ├──► report: human-readable projections
      └──► later phases: CBOM import/export, posture linter, disclosure views

The IR represents facts and evidence; answer generation, linting, and CBOM exchange are consumers. JSON Schema validates the wire contract and stays within the static-type profile: no oneOf/anyOf/allOf/not, homogeneous arrays, explicit discriminated fields for polymorphism.

docs.title: Core Model
docs.text:
type Spec struct {
    SpecVersion     string           `json:"specVersion"`
    Metadata        Metadata         `json:"metadata,omitempty"`
    System          SystemRef        `json:"system"`
    Scope           Scope            `json:"scope,omitempty"`
    Implementations []Implementation `json:"implementations,omitempty"`
    Algorithms      []Algorithm      `json:"algorithms,omitempty"`
    Uses            []Use            `json:"uses,omitempty"`
    Claims          []Claim          `json:"claims,omitempty"`
    Evidence        []Evidence       `json:"evidence,omitempty"`
}

docs.title: Spec versioning, metadata, and system identity
docs.text:
specVersion carries the semver of the spec format (not the described system): v0.1 files carry "0.1.0". Additive format changes bump minor; breaking changes bump major. Tooling accepts any file whose major version it understands.

type Metadata struct {
    Name        string `json:"name,omitempty"`
    Description string `json:"description,omitempty"`
    CreatedAt   string `json:"createdAt,omitempty"` // RFC 3339
    UpdatedAt   string `json:"updatedAt,omitempty"`
}

type SystemRef struct {
    ID   string `json:"id"`
    Name string `json:"name,omitempty"`
}

SystemRef is deliberately minimal in v0.1 — an opaque system ID plus display name. A structured family-wide identifier scheme is a later shared-primitives decision; adopting one must not break v0.1 files (the ID stays a string).

Every spec states exactly what it describes — which system, release, environment, and components. This matters when a customer asks about a released version while the main branch already contains unreleased crypto changes.

type Scope struct {
    Release     string   `json:"release,omitempty"`
    Environment string   `json:"environment,omitempty"`
    Components  []string `json:"components,omitempty"`
}

docs.title: ID and reference conventions
docs.text:
Object IDs are lowercase kebab-case strings with a type prefix, unique within the spec:

impl:<slug>        e.g. impl:go-stdlib-crypto
algorithm:<slug>   e.g. algorithm:sha-256
use:<slug>         e.g. use:artifact-integrity
claim:<slug>       e.g. claim:sha256-artifact-integrity
evidence:<slug>    e.g. evidence:update-verify-source

Reference fields (algorithmRef, implementationRef, evidenceRefs, targetRefs) hold these IDs verbatim. validate enforces that each ID carries the prefix matching its object type and that every reference points at an object of the expected type. roadmapRefs are the exception: they are opaque external identifiers, never resolved by this module.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
Libraries are only one implementation mechanism, so the concept is Implementation with a type vocabulary:

library | runtime | operating-system | cloud-provider | kms | hsm | tpm |
database | service | hardware | external

type Implementation struct {
    ID               string    `json:"id"`
    Type             string    `json:"type"`
    Name             string    `json:"name"`
    Version          string    `json:"version,omitempty"`
    Provider         string    `json:"provider,omitempty"`
    Capabilities     []string  `json:"capabilities,omitempty"`     // what it CAN do
    UsedCapabilities []string  `json:"usedCapabilities,omitempty"` // what this system DOES with it
    Lifecycle        Lifecycle `json:"lifecycle,omitempty"`
    EvidenceRefs     []string  `json:"evidenceRefs,omitempty"`
}

Capabilities ≠ UsedCapabilities is the key anti-hallucination control: a scanner or LLM must never turn "the library supports X" into "the product uses X." validate enforces usedCapabilities ⊆ capabilities and every entry in usedCapabilities should be justified by at least one Use.

docs.title: Algorithm
docs.text:
A normalized registry describing what each primitive is — never how the system uses it (that is Use).

type Algorithm struct {
    ID        string    `json:"id"`
    Name      string    `json:"name"`      // e.g. "SHA-256", "AES-256-GCM"
    Class     string    `json:"class"`
    Standard  string    `json:"standard,omitempty"` // e.g. "FIPS 180-4"
    KeySize   int       `json:"keySize,omitempty"`
    Lifecycle Lifecycle `json:"lifecycle,omitempty"`
}

Class vocabulary:

hash | mac | symmetric-encryption | authenticated-encryption |
asymmetric-encryption | signature | kdf | password-hash |
key-agreement | kem | randomness

docs.title: Use — the heart of the spec
docs.text:
type Use struct {
    ID                string        `json:"id"`
    Purpose           string        `json:"purpose"`
    Description       string        `json:"description,omitempty"`
    AlgorithmRef      string        `json:"algorithmRef"`
    ImplementationRef string        `json:"implementationRef,omitempty"`
    Component         string        `json:"component,omitempty"`
    Data              *DataContext  `json:"data,omitempty"`          // classification of the protected data
    Configuration     *UseConfig    `json:"configuration,omitempty"` // salted, iterations, parameters
    Locations         []Location    `json:"locations,omitempty"`     // source / config / deployment locators
    Standards         []string      `json:"standards,omitempty"`
    Lifecycle         Lifecycle     `json:"lifecycle,omitempty"`
    RoadmapRefs       []string      `json:"roadmapRefs,omitempty"`
    EvidenceRefs      []string      `json:"evidenceRefs,omitempty"`
}

One Use record answers many differently-worded questions: which hashes? (algorithmRef) — why? (purpose) — where? (component, locations) — salted? (configuration) — which implementation? (implementationRef) — prove it (evidenceRefs).

Purpose is a closed vocabulary (enforced by validate), with other + description as the escape hatch so authors never invent near-synonyms:

integrity | confidentiality | authentication | signing | key-derivation |
credential-protection | randomness | other

Supporting types:

type UseConfig struct {
    Salted     *bool             `json:"salted,omitempty"`     // nil = not documented, false = explicitly unsalted
    Iterations int               `json:"iterations,omitempty"` // work factor where applicable
    Parameters map[string]string `json:"parameters,omitempty"` // named parameter set, e.g. argon2 memory/threads, AES mode
}

type DataContext struct {
    Classification string `json:"classification"` // e.g. customer-data, credentials, software-artifact, telemetry
    Description    string `json:"description,omitempty"`
}

type Location struct {
    Type       string `json:"type"` // source | config | deployment | runtime
    Repository string `json:"repository,omitempty"`
    Path       string `json:"path,omitempty"`
    Symbol     string `json:"symbol,omitempty"`
}

UseConfig carries the parameters questionnaires ask about; for password hashing this is where KDF parameters live. Common parameters get explicit fields (salted, iterations); everything else goes in parameters, a homogeneous map[string]string — allowed under the static-type profile (fixed value type, no map[string]any), following the same precedent as the family's earlier specs. The tri-state *bool on salted distinguishes "explicitly unsalted" from "not documented," which matters for answer policies.

docs.title: Claim, Evidence, Verification
docs.text:
Verification lives on claims only — deliberately. Inventory objects (implementations, algorithms, uses) carry evidenceRefs but no verification status of their own; the claim is the unit that gets verified, and one claim can cover several objects via targetRefs. Implementers must not add per-object verification fields: two verification surfaces would let an object's status and its covering claim's status disagree, and consumers would not know which to trust.

Every significant assertion is a claim supported by evidence and carrying a verification state:

type Claim struct {
    ID           string       `json:"id"`
    Type         string       `json:"type"` // e.g. "crypto-usage"
    Statement    string       `json:"statement"`
    TargetRefs   []string     `json:"targetRefs,omitempty"` // uses/implementations/algorithms this claim covers
    Verification Verification `json:"verification"`
    EvidenceRefs []string     `json:"evidenceRefs,omitempty"`
}

type Evidence struct {
    ID         string     `json:"id"`
    Type       string     `json:"type"`
    Repository string     `json:"repository,omitempty"`
    Path       string     `json:"path,omitempty"`
    Symbol     string     `json:"symbol,omitempty"`
    URI        string     `json:"uri,omitempty"`
    Provenance Provenance `json:"provenance,omitempty"`
}

type Verification struct {
    Status     string `json:"status"`
    Method     string `json:"method,omitempty"`
    VerifiedBy string `json:"verifiedBy,omitempty"`
    VerifiedAt string `json:"verifiedAt,omitempty"` // RFC 3339
}

Evidence type vocabulary:

source-code | dependency | configuration | iac | runtime-observation |
tls-scan | sbom | cbom | cloud-configuration | certificate | test |
documentation | human-attestation | vendor-documentation

Verification state machine:

discovered → inferred → review-required → verified → attested

Not every fact must reach attested, but downstream consumers can apply policies over the state:

verified / attested  → state as fact
inferred             → qualify or request review
discovered           → supporting evidence only
unknown              → "not currently documented"
conflicting          → block and request review

validate rejects statuses outside the vocabulary; transition ordering is advisory in v0.1 (any state may be recorded), with transition auditing left to tooling that writes the spec.

docs.title: Review, expectation and operating mode (planned, v0.2)
docs.text:
These additions serve producers of declared facts: statements about cryptography that the producer does not itself enforce (an edge TLS configuration, a database connection policy). They keep a declaration from being read as current fact after it has stopped being reviewed.

Review fields. Verification gains three optional fields, still on claims only (see above):

type Verification struct {
    // ...existing fields...
    ReviewBy   string `json:"reviewBy,omitempty"`   // RFC 3339 full-date: deadline for the next review
    ReviewedAt string `json:"reviewedAt,omitempty"` // RFC 3339 timestamp: when a person last reaffirmed the claim
    ReviewedBy string `json:"reviewedBy,omitempty"` // person or team; defaults to VerifiedBy when absent
}
  • verifiedAt is when the status was reached; reviewedAt is when a person last looked at it and reaffirmed it without changing the status. A reaffirmation does not claim re-verification.
  • Expiry is derived, not stored. A consumer evaluating at time T treats a claim whose reviewBy is before T as review-required, and the stored status is unchanged. The file does not change meaning as the clock moves, and the diff layer does not report the passage of time as a change.
  • validate rejects a reviewBy earlier than reviewedAt, and warns on a claim past its reviewBy as of the evaluation time (--as-of, defaulting to now).

Policy, expectation and actual. Three things are kept distinct:

Term Meaning Where it lives Policy The floor. Generic, applies to every system. The lint policy (Phase 7), never in the spec Expectation What this boundary is declared to be. Specific, with an owner. At or above the floor. A spec object Actual What was observed. Evidence (tls-scan, runtime-observation) 
policy (floor)  <=  expectation (declared target)  <=  actual (observed)
  • An Expectation is an inventory object with an owner, the object it applies to (a protocol, protection or external boundary), its attributes, and evidenceRefs pointing at where the real configuration lives. Its review date lives on the claim that covers it, not on the object, so the single verification surface rule holds.
  • Attributes take two forms. Ordered attributes (a TLS version, a key size) are minimums; the expectation must be greater than or equal to the policy minimum. Set-valued attributes (cipher suites, key-exchange groups) are allow-sets; the expectation must be a subset of the policy's set.
  • A boundary with no expectation is held to the policy directly.
  • An expectation below the floor is a waiver. It must carry a reason and an owner, and its covering claim must carry reviewBy. The linter reports it as a conditional pass until the review date and as a failure after it.
  • The three comparisons give three results: actual below policy is a violation; actual below expectation but above policy is drift; an expectation below policy is an exception.

Operating mode. An implementation records operatingMode (for example approved-algorithms-only versus standard) and, for a cryptographic module, its name, version and validation reference. A claim that a system runs in an approved-only mode then points at the implementation that states it.

Algorithm profile. A use records the named algorithmProfile enforced for it (for example fips or standard) and the implementation that defines it. It is deliberately not called profile alone: lint profiles (Phase 7) are evaluation expectations over a whole spec and are a different concept.

Key state is a summary, not a record per version. Key classes carry their class and policy (algorithm, storage, rotation interval). Current state is carried as a dated claim ("all versions within policy as of T; current version N") backed by verified evidence. The spec holds no row per key version, which would change with every rotation and drown the diff layer in noise; live state belongs to the system that manages the keys.

docs.title: Shared primitives (local now, family later)
docs.text:
type Lifecycle struct {
    Status     string `json:"status"` // proposed | planned | in-progress | available | deprecated | retired | cancelled
    Introduced string `json:"introduced,omitempty"`
    Deprecated string `json:"deprecated,omitempty"`
    Removed    string `json:"removed,omitempty"`
}

type Provenance struct {
    Method     string `json:"method"` // static-analyzer | llm-analyzer | sbom-import | scanner | developer | security-review
    Analyzer   string `json:"analyzer,omitempty"`
    AnalyzedAt string `json:"analyzedAt,omitempty"`
}

Lifecycle, Evidence, Provenance, Verification, and ID/reference conventions are shared-primitive candidates for the whole spec family. They are defined locally in this module for v0.1; extraction into a shared family root module is a deliberate later decision, deferred until at least a second family member needs them — small shared schemas, no lockstep versioning.

Planning stays out of the spec. Objects may carry roadmapRefs (opaque roadmap-item IDs); target dates, dependencies, and status of planned work live in roadmap tooling. This prevents the spec from becoming a project-management format and prevents consumers from converting "planned" into "supported."

Secrets invariant: the model describes key classes and management practices (post-v0.1 phases); no field may hold key material, secret values, or operational credentials.

Post-v0.1 model notes. The Phase 4 key-management model carries explicit standards-conformance fields on key classes and key-management providers (e.g. NIST SP 800-57, KMIP, PKCS#11, X9 family), so the key-management techniques and standards a system supports are answerable from the IR, not prose. The Phase 8 crypto-RAS model spans reliability, availability, and serviceability as separate categories — including serviceability facts like cryptographic audit logging, crypto health checks, and automated renewal — so each category is answerable independently.

docs.title: Validation Rules
docs.text:
Shipped in v0.1 as application-level rules over one schema:

referential integrity   → algorithmRef / implementationRef / evidenceRefs / targetRefs resolve
capability containment  → usedCapabilities ⊆ capabilities per implementation,
                          enforced only when capabilities are enumerated (a
                          managed KMS/HSM may declare usage without listing its
                          full capability set)
usage justification     → each usedCapability referenced by at least one Use (warning)
vocabulary conformance  → lifecycle status, verification status, algorithm class,
                          implementation type, evidence type, use purpose, location
                          type within controlled vocabularies
id conventions          → type-prefixed IDs (impl:/algorithm:/use:/claim:/evidence:);
                          references resolve to objects of the expected type
uniqueness              → object IDs unique within the spec
evidence expectation    → verified/attested claims must carry evidenceRefs

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
# v0.1
cryptospec validate <crypto.json>
cryptospec report <crypto.json>          # human-readable internal summary

# later phases
cryptospec cbom import|export ...
cryptospec lint <crypto.json> [--profile ...]
cryptospec report <crypto.json> --view internal|auditor|customer|public

Library-first: all capability lives in importable packages; cmd/cryptospec is a thin adapter. The cli package exposes:

cli.NewRootCommand() // standalone: cryptospec ...
cli.NewCommand()     // mountable:  <family-cli> crypto ...

so a future family aggregate CLI mounts this module with one import and one AddCommand().

docs.title: Repository Layout
docs.text:
systemspec-crypto/
├── cryptospec/     # core types: spec, implementation, algorithm, use, claim, evidence,
│                   # lifecycle, provenance, verification
├── validate/       # referential integrity + semantic rules
├── schema/         # generated *.schema.json + //go:embed + gen/ (go:build ignore) + tools.go
├── cli/            # cobra command constructors (NewRootCommand / NewCommand)
├── cmd/cryptospec/ # thin main
├── examples/       # fixture corpus (valid/invalid) + dogfood spec
└── docs/specs/initiatives/INIT-SYSTEMSPECCRYPTO-001/

Later phases add cbom/, lint/, policy/, report/.

docs.title: Schema Pipeline, Conformance & Testing
docs.text:
• Go structs → invopop/jsonschema → schema/*.schema.json, linted by schemakit lint --property-case camelCase in CI, embedded via //go:embed.
  • tools.go with //go:build tools blank imports so go mod tidy keeps the generator's deps (standard gen/main.go pattern).
  • Fixture corpus (examples/fixtures/{valid,invalid}) exercised by both the Go validator and JSON Schema validation; round-trip test Go → JSON → schema-validate → Go with semantic equality.
  • The dogfood spec (a real Go application, modeled end to end) doubles as the authoring-UX test: if modeling a real system feels painful, the schema changes, not the example.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Cobra (CLI), invopop/jsonschema (schema generation), grokify/schemakit (lint, dev/CI tool). Verify latest versions before adding. No dependency on CycloneDX tooling until the CBOM bridge phase; no runtime dependency on other family specs — references are by ID/URI.
